title: A moment obstruction and minimal-degree polynomial nonconforming Stokes elements on tetrahedra
shortTitle: Why fourth-order tetrahedral Stokes elements need a sextic
oneLine: Answers the open question of Balazi, Allaire, Jolivet and Omnes: no fifteen quintics complete a fourth-order moment-based Stokes element on tetrahedra, because the 50 moments satisfy a hidden relation on all quintics; one sextic repairs it, and for every order degree n+2 misses exactly (n−1)(n−2)/2 directions while degree n+3 always works.
abstract: Nonconforming finite elements for slow viscous (Stokes) flow are often specified by moments: averages of the velocity against polynomials on each face and inside each cell. Balazi, Allaire, Jolivet and Omnes (Numerical Methods for PDEs, 2025) built tetrahedral elements of second and third order this way and left open whether a fourth-order element can be obtained by adding fifteen quintic polynomials to the quartics. This paper shows that it cannot: an alternating face functional vanishes on every quintic but equals 1/34650 on the Vandermonde sextic of the barycentric coordinates, so the 50 moments are dependent on all quintics, and that one sextic repairs the defect, giving a 50-dimensional element independent of vertex numbering. For face moments of degree n and cell moments of degree n−1, the polynomials of degree n+2 invisible to all moments form a seven-dimensional space with an explicit basis of Jacobi and Legendre ridges for every n. Hence degree n+2 suffices only for n=1,2; for n≥3 exactly (n−1)(n−2)/2 moment directions are missing and degree n+3 is necessary and sufficient, for single-cell polynomial spaces containing all polynomials of degree n+1. Numbering-free elements with the fewest top-degree functions are proved to exist for every n, given explicitly for n=4,5 and checked for an explicit family up to n=8. On triangles no extra degree is ever needed; on higher-dimensional simplices sufficiency of degree n+3 is conjectured beyond checked cases. A numerical Stokes test shows rates consistent with fourth-order convergence, with computed discrete inf-sup values 0.40–0.37 on four meshes. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: The fourth-order question is answered in the negative: an alternating face functional vanishes on every quintic and equals 1/34650 on the Vandermonde sextic Δ₄ = ∏(λⱼ − λᵢ), so no 15 quintics complete the element (Proposition 3.2, proof; exact).

For every n the moments are injective on P_{n+1}, their kernel on P_{n+2} is exactly seven-dimensional with an explicit Jacobi/Legendre ridge basis, they miss (n−1)(n−2)/2 directions on P_{n+2} and are surjective on P_{n+3}; the minimum degree is n+2 for n=1,2 and n+3 for n≥3 (Theorem 2.1, proof).

A 50-dimensional fourth-order element with one sextic, invariant under vertex relabelling and minimal in degree and number of sextic directions (Corollary 5.8, proof); at least (n−1)(n−2)/2 top-degree directions are needed and numbering-free elements attaining this exist for every n (Corollary 5.2, Theorem 5.4, proof), explicit for n=4,5 and checked for Δ₄P_{n−3} up to n=8 (exact computation).

On triangles no extra degree is ever needed (Corollary 6.3, proof); on d-simplices the kernel dimension and deficit have closed forms (proof), degree n+3 is checked for d=4,5,6 in listed cases (exact computation) and conjectured for d≥4 in general.

A Stokes test with the fourth-order element shows rates consistent with fourth-order convergence and computed discrete inf-sup values 0.40–0.37 for N=1–4 (numerical); mesh independence comes from the Fortin argument (proof).

narration: Why fourth-order tetrahedral Stokes elements need a sextic. An Evidence Press briefing. Engineers simulate slow, sticky flows, such as blood in small vessels or oil in porous rock, by cutting space into small tetrahedra and approximating the flow in each one by a polynomial. The recipe for one cell is called a finite element. A popular way to keep velocity and pressure stable is to describe each cell by its moments: averages of the velocity against simple polynomials on each face and inside the cell. For this to work, the moments must pick out exactly one polynomial from the chosen space, and the space should use the lowest degree possible, because higher degree costs more computing time. In 2025, Balazi, Allaire, Jolivet and Omnes built elements of second and third order in this way. For fourth order they needed fifteen extra polynomials of degree five, tested millions of random choices, found none, and asked whether any choice exists. This paper shows that none does. On every polynomial of degree five, the fifty moments obey one hidden relation, revealed by a short symmetry argument, so they can never be independent. A single polynomial of degree six, the product of the six differences of the tetrahedron's barycentric coordinates, breaks the relation and gives a fourth-order element that does not depend on how the vertices are numbered. More generally, for every order the paper finds exactly seven polynomials that the moments cannot see. As a result, the natural degree works only for the two lowest orders and then falls short by a growing, exactly known number of directions, while one degree higher always works. The paper proves that symmetric elements with the fewest extra functions exist for every order, and shows that on triangles no extra degree is ever needed. A numerical test of the new element shows error rates consistent with fourth-order convergence. Some statements in four or more dimensions remain conjectures. This is an anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, not peer reviewed or independently reproduced. Published on 22 October 2026, its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

decisionObject.description: Answer to the open question of Balazi, Allaire, Jolivet and Omnes (2025) on quintic enrichment of the fourth-order tetrahedral moment element, with the exact kernel of face-and-cell moments on P_{n+2} for every n, the sharp minimal degree, minimal enrichment counts with symmetric elements, a d-simplex analysis and an explicit fourth-order element with a numerical Stokes test.
decisionObject.scope: Face moments against P_n and cell moments against P_{n-1} on a tetrahedron; single-cell polynomial spaces containing P_{n+1}; no claim about split-cell, nonpolynomial or virtual element spaces, pressure robustness, p-uniform stability or solver speed; d≥4 sufficiency of degree n+3 conjectural beyond checked cases.
